questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: A courtroom once treated a confident eyewitness identification as close to definitive proof, since jurors found it intuitively hard to imagine someone misremembering a face they claim to have seen clearly. Decades of controlled memory experiments have complicated this assumption considerably: confidence and accuracy turn out to be only loosely related, and an eyewitness can express complete certainty about an identification later proven, through independent evidence, to be entirely wrong. Some courts have responded by requiring juries to be explicitly warned that confidence is not a reliable proxy for accuracy, a warning that measurably reduces wrongful convictions built on eyewitness testimony alone.

options.text: Why Eyewitness Testimony Should Never Be Permitted in Court
Why Eyewitness Confidence Is a Poor Proxy for Actual Accuracy
A History of Jury Selection Procedures
Why Jurors Always Distrust Confident Witnesses
How Courts Train Witnesses to Testify Accurately

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A country that sees a wave of skilled workers emigrate abroad is often assumed to suffer a straightforward, one-directional loss of talent, a narrative economists call brain drain. Longitudinal studies of specific emigrant cohorts complicate this narrative considerably: a meaningful share of emigrants who train and work abroad for a decade or two eventually return, bringing back both accumulated expertise and international professional networks the origin country would never have developed on its own, a reverse flow some economists now call brain circulation rather than brain drain. Whether a given wave of emigration nets out as a loss or a long-term gain, it turns out, depends heavily on how strong the incentive to return eventually becomes.

options.text: the legal requirements for gaining permanent residency abroad
how emigration can eventually become brain circulation rather than a one-directional loss of talent
the total number of skilled workers who emigrate annually
why some countries restrict skilled emigration through policy
a comparison of two specific countries' emigration rates

options.text: the architectural techniques used in modern public housing
how misjudging a building's remaining lifespan can lead to costlier decisions in either direction
the total cost of building new public housing nationwide
why residents typically oppose renovation over demolition
a comparison of two specific cities' housing policies

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: Employers who once assumed staff needed to be physically present in an office to be genuinely productive have had to revise that assumption considerably after several years of data from employees who telecommute full time. Output, measured by completed tasks rather than hours logged, turned out to hold steady or even rise for many roles once the daily commute and office interruptions were removed. This does not mean every task benefits equally: roles requiring frequent spontaneous collaboration still show a measurable cost when done remotely, suggesting the real lesson is not that offices are obsolete, but that the assumption linking physical presence to productivity was true for some roles and false for others all along.

options.text: Telecommuting always produces higher output than working in a physical office.
Whether physical presence genuinely improves productivity depends on the specific role, not a universal rule.
Every role requiring collaboration is better performed in a physical office.
Employers were always correct that offices are essential for all roles.
Commuting has no measurable effect on employee output whatsoever.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
I spent my first year as a small-business owner treating every minor supplier delay as a genuine misfortune worth panicking over, convinced that any disruption at all would be the one that finally sank the shop. My accountant, reviewing a full year of these panics after the fact, pointed out that not a single one had actually threatened the business's survival; each had simply required a delayed order, a substitute supplier, or a few apologetic emails to customers. What had felt, in the moment, like a series of near-catastrophes turned out, in hindsight, to be the perfectly ordinary texture of running any small business. I still feel a flicker of the old panic when a shipment is delayed, but I no longer mistake that flicker for actual danger.

Statements
(a) The writer initially treated every minor supplier delay as a genuine crisis.
(b) The accountant found that at least one delay had genuinely threatened the business's survival.
(c) Resolving most delays required only a substitute supplier or an apologetic email.
(d) The writer now recognises the delays as ordinary rather than catastrophic, in hindsight.
(e) The writer no longer feels any reaction at all when a shipment is delayed.
(f) The accountant reviewed a full year of the writer's reactions to disruptions.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Firms that formally pair new hires with a senior mentor report measurably lower first-year turnover than firms that leave new hires to find informal guidance on their own, a pattern two competing explanations attempt to account for. One explanation holds that a formal mentor simply transmits practical, role-specific knowledge faster than trial and error alone would allow, shortening the painful early period during which a new hire feels incompetent. A second, competing explanation instead proposes that the mentorship relationship itself, independent of any specific knowledge transmitted, signals to the new hire that the organisation is invested in their long-term success, and it is this signal of investment, not the practical content, that actually reduces the urge to quit early.

options.text: The first explanation attributes lower turnover to faster transmission of practical, role-specific knowledge.
The first explanation suggests mentorship shortens the painful early period of feeling incompetent.
The second explanation claims the specific knowledge transmitted is what actually reduces turnover.
The second explanation attributes lower turnover to a signal of organisational investment in the new hire.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same pattern of lower first-year turnover.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the underlined phrase "the correlation trap"?
questions.context: Two variables can correlate strongly across an entire population without either one causing the other, a confusion researchers call _the correlation trap_: cities with more ice cream vendors also tend to have higher drowning rates, not because ice cream causes drowning, but because both independently increase during warmer months. Analysts who treat a strong correlation alone as sufficient evidence of a causal relationship risk building policy on a coincidence rather than a genuine mechanism.

options.text: two variables that correlate strongly must always share a direct causal relationship
mistaking a strong correlation for proof of causation can lead to flawed conclusions
ice cream consumption is a leading cause of drowning incidents worldwide
correlated variables can never share any underlying common cause
policy should never be based on any statistical evidence whatsoever

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: A besieged fortress with sufficient stored food and water can, in principle, outlast an attacking army indefinitely, since the besieging force must itself maintain a costly supply line to feed its own troops for as long as the siege continues. Historians studying prolonged sieges note that the besieging commander's real constraint was rarely the fortress's defences themselves, but the besieging army's own capacity to sustain a supply chain over months or years without the campaign becoming more costly than whatever the fortress was actually worth capturing. Many historically famous sieges ended not through a breach of the walls, but through negotiated surrender once both sides recognised the campaign had become unsustainable for the attacker.
